intro.title: Describe what happened with concrete details
paragraphs: An observation is a description of a specific event using details that someone could see, hear, quote, or count. Adding time, place, and exact words can make an account easier to understand and revisit. Research on concrete language and behavioral observation informs this guide [2], [3], [9].

Concrete details do not make your feelings, interpretation, or account of harm less real. They also do not prove another person’s intent. Use them as an additional layer when useful, not as a test you have to pass.

items: Recorder criterion: report only what a camera/microphone could capture (verbatim words, visible actions, measurable outcomes). Behavioral observation emphasizes observable units to aid reliability [9].
Time- and context-bound: specify when/where (e.g., “On Tue 15:10 in the team room…”). Concreteness improves comprehension and reduces ambiguity [2].
Avoid absolutes (“always/never/constantly”): prefer frequency, duration, or counts [3].
No mind-reading or motive attributions (e.g., “to hurt me,” “on purpose”): hostile-attribution tendencies relate to aggressive/negative responding [10], [11].
Quantify when feasible: counts, durations, latency, intensity (e.g., decibels). Linguistic abstraction inflates inference; measurables support shared description [1].

content.html: Observations describe events; other components (feelings/needs/requests) are handled elsewhere in the app. Separating description from evaluation aligns with evidence on perspective-taking/I-language [5].

items: Anchor the scene: “On [DATE] at [TIME] in [PLACE], …”. Concreteness advantage [2].
Describe only what was sensed: “I saw/heard [ACTOR] [ACTION/WORDS].” Behavioral observation favors observable units [9].
Quote verbatim when feasible: “[Exact words].” Wording influences blame inferences; direct quotes minimize reinterpretation [12].
Quantify: “[N times / for M minutes / on D dates / ~latency].” Replace vague adverbs with measurable data [3].
Remove evaluations: omit trait adjectives and “too/should” adverbs; substitute the underlying observable behavior. Language framing affects judgment [12].
Remove intent clauses (e.g., “to annoy me”). Hostile intent attributions are linked with negative responding; keep to what occurred [10].

content.html: Template: “On [DATE] at [TIME] in [PLACE], I saw/heard [ACTOR] [ACTION/WORDS]. This occurred [COUNT/DURATION/LATENCY].”

items: Absolutes: flag “always/never/constantly/every time.” Prompt for timeframe and count [2].
Trait labels: flag “rude, selfish, careless, disrespectful, aggressive, lazy,” etc. Prompt: “Describe the exact behavior instead” [12].
Mind-reading: flag “on purpose,” “to hurt me,” “because you don’t care.” Prompt: “Omit intent; report the observable act” [10].
Causation claims without evidence: flag “for no reason,” “made me,” unless tied to a measurable outcome. Encourage sticking to recorded events.
Perspective-taking for later steps: I-language and checking understanding are associated with less defensive escalation [5].

items.observation: “In the past two weeks, you arrived 5–15 minutes after our agreed time on three occasions.”
items.why: Replaces global language with time-bound frequency; concreteness improves agreement [2].

items.observation: “Janice logged 62 on-site hours this week, including Saturday.”
items.why: Removes evaluative adverb; supplies measurable quantity [3].

items.evaluation: “He left the party to hurt me.”
items.observation: “He left the party without saying goodbye at 9:10 p.m.”
items.why: Strips motive attribution; hostile-attribution research cautions against inferred intent [10].

items.observation: “During the 2:00–2:15 agenda item, while I was speaking, you interrupted twice (timestamps 08:12 and 09:47).”
items.why: Replaces trait with event-bounded counts; wording shapes perceived blame [12].

sections.label: Measurement
sections.title: Measurement Concepts: Operational Definitions, ABC, Agreement

content.text: This section summarizes commonly used measurement concepts that may inform personal or professional record-keeping in observational work.

items: Operational definitions with exemplars/non-examples [9].
ABC recording with timestamps; where feasible, use continuous measures (count, duration, latency) [13], [14].
Inter-observer agreement (IOA) on a sample of observations; consider statistics appropriate to the data (e.g., kappa) [15], [16].
Audit for observer drift and recalibrate using reference clips/exemplars [15].

content.html: Why this tab exists. Writing low-inference observations is easier when users understand why neutral, time-bound description matters in relationships. This tab collates open-access research on frequently studied psychological needs. It does not prescribe which needs you have. Its purpose is to show how clear description can support later steps (like identifying feelings/needs) by creating a shared factual baseline. For related evidence on perspective-taking and language use in communication, see: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5961625/.

items: What you’re looking at. Short summaries plus raw-URL links to readable, evidence-based sources (open-access reviews/advisories/articles). The full URLs are included so you can verify them yourself.

How this connects to observational skill. Neutral, time-bound description can reduce ambiguity and perceived social threat, which may make collaboration on next steps easier. This general idea aligns with research on needs commonly discussed in interpersonal settings—autonomy, competence, belonging, trust, and safety. See: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5050353/; https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/topics/basic-psychological-needs/; https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21058850/; https://www.dignityhealth.org/articles/how-human-connection-can-relieve-stress.

content.text: Autonomy & competence. Research on basic psychological needs suggests people benefit when they can make informed, self-directed choices and feel effective in their actions. Clear, low-inference description helps establish a shared situation model that can support agency and planning. Sources: https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC5050353/; https://selfdeterminationtheory.org/topics/basic-psychological-needs/.

Belonging / social connection. Neutral description can lower perceived social threat and open space for cooperation, which is relevant given public-health summaries linking social connection to well-being. Source: https://www.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/surgeon-general-social-connection-advisory.pdf.

Trust & safety. Language that avoids motive attributions and global labels is less likely to be received as threatening. Evidence connecting interpersonal trust with stress physiology provides useful context for why non-judging description can feel safer. Sources: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/21058850/; https://www.dignityhealth.org/articles/how-human-connection-can-relieve-stress.

items: Memory/measurement: observations depend on recall or recording fidelity; contemporaneous notes/quotes provide clearer records [9].
Intent is not adjudicated by observation: avoid hostile attributions [10].
Cultural/linguistic nuance: perceptions of “neutral” phrasing can vary; invite verification of wording.
Scope: this guide summarizes research and provides structured prompts; it does not determine clinical reliability or outcomes.

mobile.title: Observation mini-guide
intro: Tap a card for research-backed pointers. The full desktop guide stays available if you rotate or switch to a larger screen.

sections.title: What counts as an observation
sections.description: Describe the event before deciding what it meant.

items: Start with visible actions, exact words, and results someone could notice [9].
Add when and where it happened if those details are available [2].
Use a count, duration, or frequency when the amount matters. An estimate is fine [3].
Your interpretation can stay. If it matters, also add the details that led you to it.

content.html: This is a writing aid, not a truth test. A concrete description can sit beside your feelings and interpretation.

sections.title: A simple writing recipe
sections.description: Use as much of this structure as helps.

items: Begin with the moment: “On [DATE] at [TIME] in [PLACE]…” [2].
Add what you noticed: “I saw or heard [PERSON] [ACTION OR WORDS].” [9].
Use the exact words when you remember them. Quotation marks show what was said directly.
Add how many times or how long when it matters [3].
If you include a judgment or possible motive, add the details that led you there.

content.html: Optional template: “On [DATE] at [TIME] in [PLACE], I saw or heard [PERSON] [ACTION OR WORDS] [COUNT OR DURATION].”

sections.title: Why a word may be highlighted
sections.description: Highlights invite more detail; they do not mark your words wrong.

items: Words such as “always” or “often” may prompt you for a timeframe, example, or count [2].
A label such as “rude” may prompt you to add the words or actions that led you to use it.
A possible motive such as “on purpose” may prompt you to add the evidence behind your conclusion [10].
Words about harm, pressure, or impact are not treated as unreal. The prompt asks only whether you want to add specific events or constraints.
You can ignore a prompt that does not fit your meaning. The app cannot understand the full context.

sections.title: From broad wording to concrete detail
sections.description: The second version adds detail without claiming the first was false.

items.observation: “In the past two weeks, you arrived 5–15 minutes after our agreed time on three occasions.”
items.why: Adds a timeframe and count [2].

items.observation: “Janice logged 62 on-site hours this week, including Saturday.”
items.why: Adds the number of hours and the relevant timeframe [3].

items.evaluation: “He left the party to hurt me.”
items.observation: “He left the party without saying goodbye at 9:10 p.m.”
items.why: Separates the visible action from a conclusion about motive [10].

items.observation: “During the 2:00–2:15 agenda item, while I was speaking, you interrupted twice (timestamps 08:12 and 09:47).”
items.why: Adds the time, action, and count behind the word “rude.”

sections.title: When an exact record matters
sections.description: Useful for shared records, programs, or research.

items: Define the action you are recording and include examples of what does and does not count [9].
Keep a dated log with counts, durations, and what happened immediately before and after [13], [14].
If more than one person is recording, compare notes to see whether you are using the same definition [15], [16].
Recheck the definition over time so the record stays consistent [15].

sections.title: What concrete detail can and cannot do
sections.description: Useful information, without promises about the outcome.

content.text: Concrete wording can make a shared event easier to remember, compare, or discuss. It cannot guarantee that people will agree about what the event meant.
A person can accurately name harm with a broad word and still choose to add concrete details. The added detail does not excuse the behavior or erase its impact.

sections.title: Limits to remember
sections.description: Use concrete details as information, not as a verdict.

items: Memory can change over time. Write down exact words or details soon afterward when accuracy matters [9].
A concrete description does not prove another person’s intent [10].
People may describe the same event differently because of viewpoint, language, culture, access, or missing information.
This guide is not a clinical assessment, legal standard, or requirement for being believed.
